newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton-Prices seen up in Pakistan, easing in India.
newsitem.headline: Cotton-Prices seen up in Pakistan, easing in India.

text.p: Pakistani cotton prices could firm next week amid conflicting talk about the size of the crop, but abundant new crop arrivals are likely to depress rates in India, dealers said on Thursday.
Karachi dealers said prices had risen this week after rumours of a shortfall in the 1996/97 (July-June) crop as spinners sought but often could not find good-quality supplies.

The All Pakistan Textile Mills Association (APTMA) said on Monday output would not exceed nine million bales, 400,000 bales short of what it says are textile industry needs of 9.4 million bales. The industry used 8.9 million bales last year.
The textile lobby wants the government to allow duty-free import of at least one million bales in 1996/97.
Maqbool Sadiq, chairman of the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA), said the demand was valid as pest attacks had eroded quality and cotton fibre strength in the new crop.
"Quality is not good after the whitefly attack," he said.
Thursday's KCA spot rates for NIAB-78 rose 11 rupees ($0.27) to 2,432.50 per maund, K-68 rose 22 rupees to 2,526 and MNH-93 rose 22 to 2,563.50. On the kerb NIAB-78 traded at 2,275-2,125.
KCA weekly cotton prices (rupees/maund, $1=40.22 rupees)
Thursday Wednesday Oct 24
In India cotton prices are likely to be under pressure as increased arrivals from the 1996/97 crop (October/September) flood the markets, traders said.
"Farmers are bringing more cotton to the markets and sentiment turned weak due to limited buying by state-run agencies," said a trader.
India's 1996/97 cotton crop is expected to be around 16 million bales, about the same as the previous year.
Spot Bengal-deshi fell 30/90 rupees to 870/890 rupees per maund (37.32 kg). Punjab saw-ginned lost 35/50 rupees to 1,590/1,650 rupees per maund for the average variety.
Gujarat Sankar-4 (long-staple) fell 900/1,100 rupees to 19,500/20,400 rupees per candy (355.56 kg).
Now arrivals are picking up and traders, noting low physical buying by millers, expected further losses.
"State-owned agencies should enter the market if the government wants to stabilise cotton prices and help farmers," said another trader.
Daily average arrivals in the northern states of Punjab and Haryana rose to 20,000-25,000 bales (170 kg each) in the week to Thursday from 16,000-18,000 bales in the previous week.
Traders said new crop arrivals in central and western India had also started.
"Prices will certainly be under pressure to move downward next week," said a trader.
